title: How to read an ingredients list without a chemistry degree
meta_description: Ingredient lists follow rules that make them readable once you know them. What the order means, where the 1% line sits, and which marketing claims mean nothing.
excerpt: The first five ingredients are most of the bottle. Everything after the 1% line is listed in any order the brand likes.
intro: Ingredient lists look deliberately impenetrable, but they follow a standard called INCI, and the rules are simple enough to learn in a few minutes. Once you know them you can tell roughly what is in a product before you buy it.

sections.heading: Order tells you concentration, until it does not
paragraphs: Ingredients are listed in descending order of concentration — until you reach ingredients present at 1% or less. Below that line, a brand may list them in any order it chooses.
This is the single most useful thing to know, because it means a hero active listed near the end could be at 0.9% or 0.01% and the label reads identically.

sections.heading: Finding the 1% line
paragraphs: There is no marker, but there is a reliable clue. Preservatives, fragrance and colourants are almost always used at well under 1%. Once you spot phenoxyethanol, sodium benzoate, parfum or a colour index number, everything from roughly that point on is a trace amount.
So if the ingredient the whole product is marketed on appears after that point, you are looking at a very small quantity of it.

sections.heading: Claims that mean nothing
paragraphs: "Chemical-free" is meaningless — water is a chemical. "Clean" and "non-toxic" have no legal definition in most markets and no agreed standard behind them.
"Dermatologist tested" tells you a test happened. It does not tell you the result. "Hypoallergenic" is similarly unregulated in many places.
None of this means a product is bad. It means the front of the pack is marketing and the back of the pack is information.

steps.title: Read the first five
steps.detail: These are the bulk of the formula. Water, an emollient, a humectant and a thickener is a normal opening for a moisturiser.
steps.tip: If the product is sold on one ingredient, check whether it is in this group.

steps.title: Locate the actives
steps.detail: Find the ingredient the marketing is about and see where it sits relative to the preservatives.
steps.tip: Sunscreens are different — active filters are declared separately with exact percentages.

steps.title: Spot the 1% line
steps.detail: Preservatives, parfum and CI colour numbers mark roughly where trace amounts begin.
steps.tip: Fragrance high in a list is common in perfumed body products and worth noting if you are sensitive.

steps.title: Ignore the front of the pack
steps.detail: Decide from the ingredient list and the price, not the claims.
steps.tip: An expensive product with a good formula and a cheap one with the same first eight ingredients often perform similarly.

faqs.a: Both are permitted at regulated concentrations and are among the more studied cosmetic ingredients. Avoiding them is a personal preference rather than a safety requirement, and 'free from' labelling is a marketing decision.

faqs.q: Why do the same products have different lists in different countries?
faqs.a: Regulations differ. The EU restricts more ingredients than the US, and colourant naming conventions vary, so brands reformulate for each market.

faqs.q: Does a shorter ingredient list mean a better product?
faqs.a: No. Short lists are easier to read, not inherently better formulated. Some very effective products are long because they include stabilisers that make the actives work.
